requirements.requirement: inventory-api runs on node1 as a managed (systemd) service
requirements.summary: A systemd unit inventory-api.service was created with Restart=always and OOMScoreAdjust=-1000, enabled, and shown active (running) both at initial deployment and after reboot with correct PID/status.

requirements.requirement: Service exposes working inventory API endpoints
requirements.summary: curl to /healthz and /inventory returned correct JSON before, during, and after the OOM event and after reboot.

requirements.requirement: A memory-hungry process drives the system out of memory
requirements.summary: A hog process was launched and grew to ~912MB RSS on a 999M/no-swap node, exhausting available memory, confirmed via free -h and ps.

requirements.requirement: Kernel OOM killer selects the memory hog, not inventory-api
requirements.summary: dmesg shows the OOM killer's candidate table with inventory-api's PID at oom_score_adj -1000 (spared) and the hog PID at oom_score_adj 0 / score 893, followed by 'Killed process 3036 (python3)' confirming only the hog was killed.

requirements.requirement: inventory-api keeps serving throughout and after the OOM event
requirements.summary: The original service PID (2409) was confirmed unchanged and /healthz and /inventory continued returning correct responses during memory exhaustion and immediately after the hog was killed.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on node1 (the only managed node)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot identity and healthy baseline were captured, the restart was acknowledged before disconnect, a different post-restart boot identity was observed (matching the fixed after-executor snapshot), and the service/API/oom-protection state was confirmed recovered afterward.

overall_summary: The executor deployed inventory-api as a systemd-managed service with OOMScoreAdjust=-1000 on node1, then directly demonstrated the required behavior: a memory hog exhausted RAM on a 999M/no-swap node, and dmesg evidence shows the kernel OOM killer selected and killed the hog (oom_score 893) while sparing inventory-api (oom_score_adj -1000), which continued serving /healthz and /inventory throughout. The single managed node's restart protocol was also completed end-to-end with a genuine boot-identity change and confirmed post-restart service/API recovery, cross-checked against the fixed after-executor snapshot. All mutations (sysctl overcommit toggle, hog script) were bounded, purposeful, and fully cleaned up or reverted.
limitations: Evidence is based solely on captured command transcripts and fixed lifecycle snapshots; no independent live verification was possible.

The before_prepare and after_prepare snapshots are identical aliases (prepare disabled), so preparer-vs-executor state separation relies entirely on the executor's own before/after captures within the timeline.

operational_hygiene.summary: Mutations were minimal and all traceable to a required purpose. The vm.overcommit_memory sysctl was temporarily set to 1 (cmd-86f80945a5444bf2) specifically to allow real memory exhaustion rather than a self-inflicted MemoryError, and was reverted to its original value 0 afterward (cmd-75ebadab90b04fb9) - a bounded, low-risk, fully-restored change. The first hog run (cmd-85c52229dc554ac2, cmd-c7ef0137abb94086) failed with a Python-level MemoryError under the default overcommit heuristic; this directly informed the sysctl adjustment rather than being an unrelated experiment. The /tmp/mem-hog.py test script and its log/pid files were removed at the end (cmd-72fb162d619f4eba partially failed due to permissions, corrected by sudo rm in cmd-fe1e8a457d054905), leaving no residue, consistent with the after_executor temp-files snapshot showing no leftover hog artifacts. No failed or conflicting services, no unsafe exposure, and package/service state matches expectations after reboot.
